html:
As you move into teaching the lesson sequence, the work of teacher-research shifts from planning to paying attention. This is the moment to notice how students engage with the texts, the writing, the talk, and the structure of the lessons: what’s working, what’s surprising, and what questions begin to surface for you. These “during teaching” reflections not only help you make sense of what’s unfolding in your own classroom, but also contribute to our shared learning community; your observations become part of the collective inquiry that helps all of us better understand how students learn through layered reading, writing, and discussion.

This is the second of the three connected discussions in this module (before, during, and after teaching). By participating in all three, you’ll complete the cycle and earn the discussion badge.

💬Reflect and Share

Join the During Teaching Discussion and share your reflection:

  • What are you noticing as you use teach the Layered Writing lesson sequence with your students? Share one or two observations about student engagement, questions, or responses that feel worth paying attention to. If you can, also include 1–2 artifacts from your classroom (pictures of student work, a snapshot of your classroom, witing in a Writer's Notebook, etc) that help capture what the lesson sequence looked like in practice.

Be sure to take a few minutes to respond to at least two other teachers’ posts to continue the conversation.

Next, you’ll continue to the third discussion, where you’ll reflect on what you’ve learned after teaching the lesson sequence.

I do not have my artifacts yet since we wrapped up this assignment today and their notes are in their notebooks, but I wanted to go ahead and reflect on this portion of the activity while my memory was still fresh. I will include my artifacts by next week once I have had a chance to grade notebooks.

During this activity, students were so engaged. They were excited to share their thoughts about the texts with their peers. The timed partner shares also kept conversations on topic, and it made me happy some students were still eager to keep sharing even when talking time was over. Students actually picked up their conversations after class and carried them on into the hallways. I was so proud!

One big realization I had was how the activity impacted my lower-level readers. I had a couple of students who really struggled to identify the claim of the texts. Those students had largely chalked the texts up to political articles and were stuck on that I must be trying to push them in some type of direction. I was able to sit down with those students, talk about the claim, talk about how the author used content to support their claims and work from there. By the time we finished these conversations, these students realized they had originally perceived the texts incorrectly and were on board, but it has made me aware of their reading comprehension in general. It led me to ask them questions about their independent reading books and Shakespeare excerpts, where I then realized they were really misunderstanding a lot of big ideas moving in those texts as well. Therefore, I am now realizing that I need to create more structural moments where students are responding to central claims and content they read that day so that I can check in on my students' reading comprehension.

Through the Layered Writing lessons with my students I have observed them being more open minded about both sides of an argument. At the beginning of the lesson I told them the topic was Fast Fashion. We had a discussion about the term fast fashion and then they wrote their thoughts about the impact of fast fashion. I gave them their first article about the impacts of fast fashion that they had to read and respond to. They wrote down their ideas and what stood out to them in the text. They picked one piece of evidence that they felt supported to the claim of the text. Then I gave them their second article that discussed a different viewpoint than the first article and they did the same for it. At the end they discussed the two articles with a peer and wrote their own claim about the impacts of fast fashion. I feel as though students better understood the text through this process and were able to have thoughtful discussions. They also were able to quickly finding relevant evidence to support their own claim.
